overview.eyebrow: A decade of changes in executive authority
overview.headline: Political Transitions Atlas
overview.introduction: Explore documented changes in who held national executive office or governing authority between 11 November 2016 and 11 November 2026. Select a country or period to see the leadership sequence, how each transfer occurred and the evidence behind it.
overview.short_description: An interactive register of executive handovers, collective leadership changes and the evidence that supports them.

cards.label: Office and authority handovers
cards.detail: Changes in the holder of a tracked executive office or governing authority.

cards.label: Collective membership changes
cards.detail: Membership changes in bodies that themselves hold national executive headship or separate head-of-state powers.

cards.label: Geographic cases researched
cards.detail: 193 UN members, the Holy See and State of Palestine, plus separately labelled Kosovo and Taiwan.

cards.detail: All relevant leadership sequences in these countries pass full-period checks under the stated definition. 21 cases still have identified gaps.

overview.release_note: Research version S013, updated on 13 November 2026. Events are recorded only through 11 November 2026.
overview.interpretation: A country may have several separately empowered executive offices, each with its own sequence. Counts therefore describe recorded office and authority changes; they are not a score of political instability, democracy or regime change.

methods.title: Geographic and time coverage
paragraphs: The atlas covers 11 November 2016 to 11 November 2026, inclusive. Its 197 geographic cases comprise the 193 United Nations members, the Holy See and State of Palestine, with Kosovo and Taiwan listed separately. Inclusion and map boundaries do not express a position on recognition or territorial claims.
Dependent territories and other disputed entities are outside this study. The observations for 2016 and 2026 cover only part of each year.

methods.title: What counts as a handover?
paragraphs: A handover is a substantive change in the person or body holding one tracked national executive office or governing authority. The study tracks heads of government, heads of state with separate executive powers, and effective governing authorities where actual control differs from formal office.

A president and a prime minister can have separate leadership sequences in the same country. A governing body can transfer authority while its chair remains in office. Related handovers are linked where established, but each change of office or authority remains a separate record.

The study excludes ceremonial offices, routine cover for travel or illness, cabinet reshuffles without a new executive head, and uninterrupted re-election or reappointment of the same holder. Substantive acting or interim successions after vacancy, removal, incapacity or collapse count however brief. Confirming an acting leader in the same role is recorded as a milestone unless the holder or authority also changes.

methods.title: Why collective changes have their own series
paragraphs: Collective records track membership changes in bodies that themselves hold national executive headship or separately empowered head-of-state authority. Simultaneous replacements within one body form one record. Ordinary cabinet reshuffles are excluded. A chair rotation counts only if distinct executive powers transfer.

The atlas contains 105 collective membership changes and 686 office and authority handovers. Each series counts a different kind of change, so their totals remain separate. A country can have collective changes even when it has no individual handovers.

methods.title: Dates and uncertainty
paragraphs: Dates refer to when authority changed hands. An election, announcement, appointment, oath and ceremonial handover can fall on different days. Each record explains the date used.

Of the 686 handovers, 614 have an exact day and 72 have a supported date interval. The collective series contains 84 exact dates and 21 intervals. An interval gives the earliest and latest supported dates for a single event. It does not describe a transition that lasted throughout that period.

Date intervals appear in a filtered view when they overlap the selected period, and remain labelled as uncertain. The annual chart shows intervals that cross calendar years separately. Its bars therefore include 684 handovers and 104 collective changes; 2 handovers and 1 collective change have cross-year intervals.

An unidentified outgoing or incoming holder remains unknown. A blank field does not establish a vacancy or an empty governing body. Uncertainty about whether a change occurred, or how many changes occurred, is recorded separately from uncertainty about its date.

methods.title: What the coverage status means
paragraphs: All 197 cases have been researched. In 176, every relevant leadership sequence has been checked for the full period. The other 21 have identified gaps in evidence or office scope. A verified event remains usable when its country's wider sequence is incomplete.

A full-period check covers the opening holder, intervening changes and continuity through 11 November 2026. It also explains vacancies and overlapping claims. Finding the same holder at both endpoints is insufficient on its own.

12 cases have evidence that no qualifying transition occurred during the study period. A zero in a filtered view does not establish that finding. Coverage is a documented research assessment, not a statistical guarantee of completeness.

There are 43 open research questions and 2 event candidates awaiting sufficient evidence. Questions can concern scope, dates or membership, so these numbers should not be added as a count of missing events. Held candidates are excluded from the totals.

methods.title: Sources and checking
paragraphs: The research uses official appointment records, constitutions, parliamentary proceedings and government chronologies, alongside contemporary reporting. Each record links to its evidence. Leadership and coup catalogues help identify possible omissions; their entries are checked before inclusion.

For each added or corrected event, a second researcher opens the supporting sources and checks the date, office, outgoing and incoming holders, mechanism and summary. Search snippets alone are insufficient. Conflicting evidence and inaccessible sources remain in the research record.

Research and review use GPT-6 Astra Pro in separate contexts. Reviewers may consult the same documents as researchers. Their agreement is therefore a check on interpretation, not independent documentary confirmation. The archive retains corrections, disagreements and unresolved candidates.

methods.title: What the latest review checked
paragraphs: S013 makes targeted evidence checks in 13 of the 21 countries with incomplete coverage. Five evidence updates received separate-agent source review. No handover, collective change, country upgrade or question closure is supported. The register remains at 686 handovers and 105 collective changes, with full-period coverage for 176 of 197 countries and 21 partial cases.

A second researcher checked the sources for every factual addition, correction and coverage upgrade adopted in this release. Unchanged findings retain their earlier source reviews. The review did not reconstruct every country afresh.

methods.title: Comparing countries and mechanisms
paragraphs: Totals depend partly on the number of executive offices tracked in each country. More recorded handovers do not by themselves establish greater political instability. Regional comparisons also reflect different numbers of countries and gaps in coverage.

Each record has one primary mechanism, with the circumstances explained in its summary and notes. Political processes can overlap. An electoral, parliamentary or constitutional label does not assess the quality of democratic institutions.

A new officeholder does not necessarily bring a new ruling party, coalition or regime. The evidence determines whether the governing group is marked changed, continued, mixed, unclear or not applicable. For 340 of 686 handovers, group change remains unclear. Those cases remain unknown.

mechanisms.label: Election handover
mechanisms.definition: A transfer of office following an election. The recorded date is the transfer, which may be later than polling day.

mechanisms.label: Parliamentary or coalition replacement
mechanisms.definition: A replacement through parliamentary or coalition processes, as explained in the record.

mechanisms.label: Same-party succession
mechanisms.definition: A replacement within the same governing party.

mechanisms.label: Constitutional succession
mechanisms.definition: A transfer under the constitutional succession rules identified in the record.

mechanisms.label: Replacement after resignation
mechanisms.definition: A successor takes office after the previous holder resigns.

mechanisms.label: Interim or caretaker succession
mechanisms.definition: A substantive succession to or from an acting, interim or caretaker executive. Routine temporary cover is excluded.

mechanisms.label: Coup or military takeover
mechanisms.definition: A transfer of executive authority through a coup or military takeover. Unsuccessful attempts that do not transfer authority are excluded.

mechanisms.label: Negotiated transition
mechanisms.definition: A transfer under a negotiated political agreement.

mechanisms.label: Restoration
mechanisms.definition: A displaced holder or authority returns to the executive role.

mechanisms.label: Hereditary succession
mechanisms.definition: A transfer of an executive office through hereditary succession.

mechanisms.label: Other mechanism
mechanisms.definition: A verified handover that falls outside the other categories. Its record explains the circumstances.

mechanisms.label: Mechanism unresolved
mechanisms.definition: The evidence does not establish a primary mechanism for the transfer.

governing_group.label: Changed
governing_group.definition: The evidence supports a change in the governing group.

governing_group.label: Continued
governing_group.definition: The evidence supports continuity of the governing group despite the handover.

governing_group.label: Mixed
governing_group.definition: Some elements of the governing group change while others continue. The record explains the combination.

governing_group.label: Unclear
governing_group.definition: The evidence does not establish whether the governing group changed.

governing_group.label: Not applicable
governing_group.definition: This group-change classification is not applied to the record.

sensitivity.title: How the definition affects the count
sensitivity.introduction: These options show how specified choices about which offices and events to include affect the totals. They filter the records without changing the underlying historical findings.

scenarios.label: Exclude temporary electoral function transfers
scenarios.detail: Omits 5 distinct handovers and 0 collective changes. Temporary electoral transfer or resumption of presidential functions while the incumbent retains the mandate. Overlapping exclusions count each record once.

scenarios.label: Exclude presidencies admitted for reserve powers
scenarios.detail: Omits 16 distinct handovers and 0 collective changes. Presidency admitted for independently exercisable reserve powers rather than ordinary general executive administration. Overlapping exclusions count each record once.

scenarios.label: Omit Nicaragua’s formal co-presidency addition
scenarios.detail: Omits 0 distinct handovers and 1 collective change. Specific legal-composition sensitivity for Nicaragua’s 2025 formal co-presidency addition. Overlapping exclusions count each record once.

scenarios.label: Exclude same-holder renewals after legal interruption
scenarios.detail: Omits 5 distinct handovers and 0 collective changes. Same holder resumes office after a documented legal interruption, including formal renewals following expiry or express termination. Overlapping exclusions count each record once.

scenarios.label: Apply all listed narrower choices
scenarios.detail: Omits 25 distinct handovers and 1 collective change. Presidency admitted for independently exercisable reserve powers rather than ordinary general executive administration; Temporary electoral transfer or resumption of presidential functions while the incumbent retains the mandate; Specific legal-composition sensitivity for Nicaragua’s 2025 formal co-presidency addition; Same holder resumes office after a documented legal interruption, including formal renewals following expiry or express termination. Overlapping exclusions count each record once.

sensitivity.limit: These comparisons concern definitions. They do not estimate missing events or give statistical uncertainty bounds.

tooltips.coverage_full: All relevant office sequences have passed checks across the stated window. This is a protocol-based assessment, not a guarantee against undiscovered events.
tooltips.coverage_partial: One or more office, authority or membership questions remain unresolved. The listed verified events are still supported.
tooltips.date_range: The handover occurred within the displayed interval. Its exact day is not established; the interval is not a duration of transition.
tooltips.no_selected_records: No admitted records match these filters. Check the country coverage status before interpreting this as continuity.
tooltips.no_transition_verified: Opening, intervening and endpoint evidence supports no in-scope transition across the full study window.
tooltips.annual: 2016 begins on 11 November; 2026 ends on 11 November. Cross-year intervals are listed separately instead of assigned to a guessed year.
tooltips.group_change: A different holder does not necessarily mean a different governing group. Unclear cases remain explicitly unknown.
tooltips.collective: One change in the membership of a governing body. Simultaneous replacements in that body are grouped. This series uses a different unit from handovers.
tooltips.count_comparison: Totals vary with the number and kind of executive offices tracked, as well as the events recorded.
